blocks.en: "But when He saw the multitudes, He was moved with compassion for them, because they were weary and scattered, like sheep having no shepherd." — Matthew 9:36 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Y viendo las multitudes, tuvo compasión de ellas; porque estaban derramadas y esparcidas como ovejas que no tienen pastor." — Mateo 9:36 (RVG)

blocks.en: 1. Moved With Compassion
blocks.es_reference: 1. Movido a Compasión

blocks.en: Matthew 9:36 (NKJV): "But when He saw the multitudes, He was moved with compassion for them, because they were weary and scattered, like sheep having no shepherd."
blocks.es_reference: Mateo 9:36 (RVG): "Y viendo las multitudes, tuvo compasión de ellas; porque estaban derramadas y esparcidas como ovejas que no tienen pastor."

blocks.en: Before Jesus ever commands us to be kind, the Gospels show us His own kindness in action. Again and again we read that "He had compassion on them." He saw the multitudes — not as a faceless crowd or a problem to be managed, but as weary, scattered people, like sheep without a shepherd — and something moved in Him. Kindness, in its deepest Christian sense, begins not with a duty we perform but with a heart that is genuinely moved by the condition of others.
blocks.es_reference: Antes de que Jesús nos mande siquiera ser bondadosos, los Evangelios nos muestran su propia bondad en acción. Una y otra vez leemos que "tuvo compasión de ellos." Vio las multitudes — no como una masa sin rostro ni un problema que administrar, sino como personas cansadas y esparcidas, como ovejas sin pastor — y algo se movió en Él. La bondad, en su sentido cristiano más hondo, comienza no con un deber que cumplimos sino con un corazón que de veras es movido por la condición de los demás.

blocks.en: This is important, because we often reduce kindness to mere politeness or good manners. But the kindness Jesus models and commands is far weightier than that. It is compassion: a heart that truly sees people in their need and is stirred to help them. The crowds were harassed and helpless, and Jesus did not look past them or grow annoyed at their demands; He was moved for them. To be kind, biblically, is to let our hearts be moved the way His was, and then to act on it.
blocks.es_reference: Esto es importante, porque a menudo reducimos la bondad a mera cortesía o buenos modales. Pero la bondad que Jesús modela y manda es mucho más pesada que eso. Es compasión: un corazón que de veras ve a las personas en su necesidad y se conmueve para ayudarlas. Las multitudes estaban acosadas y desamparadas, y Jesús no las pasó por alto ni se irritó ante sus demandas; se conmovió por ellas. Ser bondadoso, bíblicamente, es dejar que nuestro corazón sea movido como lo fue el suyo, y luego actuar.

blocks.en: 2. Compassion Means "I Feel You"
blocks.es_reference: 2. La Compasión Significa "Te Siento"

blocks.en: The word the Gospels use for Jesus' compassion is a remarkably physical one. It does not describe a mild sympathy or a passing pity; it means to be moved viscerally, from the very core of one's being. When Jesus had compassion, He felt the pain of the people in His gut. Compassion of this kind is not a tidy emotion held at arm's length; it is being so moved by another's suffering that you feel it as if it were your own.
blocks.es_reference: La palabra que los Evangelios usan para la compasión de Jesús es notablemente física. No describe una simpatía leve ni una lástima pasajera; significa ser movido visceralmente, desde el centro mismo del propio ser. Cuando Jesús tuvo compasión, sintió el dolor de la gente en sus entrañas. La compasión de esta clase no es una emoción ordenada que se sostiene a distancia; es ser tan movido por el sufrimiento de otro que lo sientes como si fuera tuyo.

blocks.en: There is a beautiful picture of this in the Spanish phrase lo siento. We translate it "I am sorry," but the words literally mean something closer to "I feel it." To say lo siento to someone in pain is to say, in effect, "I feel it with you." In settings of deep suffering, people say much the same thing — "I feel you." That is exactly what Jesus was like. He felt their pain. And so His compassion was never abstract: when people were sick, He healed them; when they were hungry, He fed them, on one occasion more than five thousand; when they were trapped in sin, He forgave them. Compassion that truly feels will always move toward the one who hurts.
blocks.es_reference: Hay una hermosa imagen de esto en la frase española lo siento. La usamos para disculparnos, pero las palabras dicen literalmente “lo siento”: siento ese dolor. Por eso es más que una disculpa: decir lo siento a alguien que sufre es decir, en efecto, “lo siento contigo”. En lugares de hondo sufrimiento, la gente dice algo muy parecido: “te siento”. Eso es exactamente como era Jesús. Sintió su dolor. Y por eso su compasión nunca fue abstracta: cuando las personas estaban enfermas, las sanó; cuando tenían hambre, las alimentó, en una ocasión a más de cinco mil; cuando estaban atrapadas en el pecado, las perdonó. La compasión que de veras siente siempre se moverá hacia el que sufre.

blocks.en: 3. The Kindness of God Toward Us
blocks.es_reference: 3. La Bondad de Dios Hacia Nosotros

blocks.en: Ephesians 4:32 (NKJV): "And be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God in Christ forgave you."
blocks.es_reference: Efesios 4:32 (RVG): "Antes sed los unos con los otros benignos, misericordiosos, perdonándoos unos a otros, como también Dios os perdonó a vosotros en Cristo."

blocks.en: We cannot understand the command to be kind until we see where Christian kindness comes from. Paul does not simply say "be kind"; he says "be kind to one another... even as God in Christ forgave you." Our kindness is meant to be a reflection and an overflow of the kindness God has already shown us. Scripture says it is the kindness of God that leads us to repentance — that we love because He first loved us, and we are kind because He was first kind to us.
blocks.es_reference: No podemos entender el mandamiento de ser bondadosos hasta que veamos de dónde viene la bondad cristiana. Pablo no dice sencillamente "sed bondadosos"; dice "sed benignos unos con otros... como también Dios os perdonó en Cristo." Nuestra bondad ha de ser un reflejo y un desbordamiento de la bondad que Dios ya nos ha mostrado. La Escritura dice que es la bondad de Dios la que nos guía al arrepentimiento — que amamos porque Él nos amó primero, y somos bondadosos porque Él fue bondadoso con nosotros primero.

blocks.en: This changes everything about how we approach the command. Kindness is not a debt we pay to earn God's favor, nor a strain we manufacture by gritted teeth. It is gratitude in action — the natural response of a heart that has been treated far more kindly than it deserved. When we remember how patient, how merciful, how tenderhearted God has been with us in Christ, kindness toward others stops feeling like a burden and starts feeling like the most reasonable thing in the world. We give what we have received.
blocks.es_reference: Esto cambia todo en cuanto a cómo abordamos el mandamiento. La bondad no es una deuda que pagamos para ganar el favor de Dios, ni una tensión que fabricamos con los dientes apretados. Es la gratitud en acción — la respuesta natural de un corazón que ha sido tratado mucho más bondadosamente de lo que merecía. Cuando recordamos cuán paciente, cuán misericordioso, cuán compasivo ha sido Dios con nosotros en Cristo, la bondad hacia los demás deja de sentirse como una carga y empieza a sentirse como lo más razonable del mundo. Damos lo que hemos recibido.

blocks.en: 4. Compassion That Acts
blocks.es_reference: 4. La Compasión Que Actúa

blocks.en: True compassion never stays a feeling; it always becomes a deed. We have already seen that when Jesus was moved with compassion, He did something about it — He healed, He fed, He forgave. Feeling sorry for people while doing nothing is not the kindness Scripture commends; it is sentiment, and sentiment costs nothing and helps no one. The kindness God calls for gets up off its chair.
blocks.es_reference: La compasión verdadera nunca se queda en sentimiento; siempre se vuelve obra. Ya hemos visto que cuando Jesús fue movido a compasión, hizo algo al respecto — sanó, alimentó, perdonó. Sentir lástima por las personas sin hacer nada no es la bondad que la Escritura elogia; es sentimentalismo, y el sentimentalismo no cuesta nada y a nadie ayuda. La bondad que Dios pide se levanta de su silla.

blocks.en: A plate and a Coke: Kindness like this is usually unspectacular and close to home. A young man named Caleb knew of a man around the corner who could not walk, so he carried a plate of food down to him — and then went back out and bought him a Coke as well. There is no grand program here, no fanfare; just a person who noticed a need nearby and met it, with a little extra thoughtfulness thrown in. Most of the kindness God asks of us looks exactly like that: seeing the person in front of us and doing the next concrete, helpful thing.
blocks.es_reference: Un plato y una Coca: La bondad como ésta suele ser poco espectacular y cercana a casa. Un joven llamado Caleb sabía de un hombre a la vuelta de la esquina que no podía caminar, así que le llevó un plato de comida — y luego salió y le compró también una Coca-Cola. No hay aquí ningún gran programa, ninguna fanfarria; solo una persona que notó una necesidad cercana y la suplió, con un poco de consideración extra de añadidura. La mayor parte de la bondad que Dios nos pide se ve exactamente así: ver a la persona frente a nosotros y hacer la siguiente cosa concreta y útil.

blocks.en: This is the genius of Christian kindness: it is available to everyone, all the time. We may not be able to feed five thousand, but we can carry a plate to a neighbor. We will not heal every sickness, but we can sit with someone who is sick. Compassion that acts does not wait for a great occasion; it takes the small occasion at hand and fills it with love.
blocks.es_reference: Ésta es la genialidad de la bondad cristiana: está al alcance de todos, todo el tiempo. Quizá no podamos alimentar a cinco mil, pero podemos llevar un plato a un vecino. No sanaremos toda enfermedad, pero podemos sentarnos con alguien que está enfermo. La compasión que actúa no espera una gran ocasión; toma la pequeña ocasión a la mano y la llena de amor.

blocks.en: 5. Kindness to the Overlooked
blocks.es_reference: 5. Bondad Hacia los Olvidados

blocks.en: James 1:27 (NKJV): "Pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their trouble, and to keep oneself unspotted from the world."
blocks.es_reference: Santiago 1:27 (RVG): "La religión pura y sin mácula delante de Dios y Padre es ésta: Visitar los huérfanos y las viudas en sus tribulaciones, y guardarse sin mancha del mundo."

blocks.en: Scripture has a special concern for the people the world tends to overlook. From the days of Moses, the widow and the orphan were placed under God's particular protection and commended to the tender care of the righteous. James goes so far as to define pure religion not by ceremony or correct opinion but by this: looking after orphans and widows in their distress. The truest test of our kindness is how we treat those who can do nothing for us in return — the people with no power, no status, and nothing to offer.
blocks.es_reference: La Escritura tiene una preocupación especial por las personas que el mundo tiende a pasar por alto. Desde los días de Moisés, la viuda y el huérfano fueron puestos bajo la protección particular de Dios y encomendados al tierno cuidado de los justos. Santiago llega a definir la religión pura no por la ceremonia ni la opinión correcta sino por esto: cuidar de los huérfanos y las viudas en su aflicción. La prueba más cierta de nuestra bondad es cómo tratamos a quienes nada pueden hacer por nosotros a cambio — las personas sin poder, sin estatus, y sin nada que ofrecer.

blocks.en: Jesus extended that same concern to the stranger, the sick, and the prisoner. "I was a stranger and you did not take Me in... I was sick and in prison and you did not visit Me," He warned — teaching that compassion shown or withheld to "the least of these" is shown or withheld to Him. Kindness, then, is not to be reserved for our friends and equals, the people who can repay us. It is to flow especially toward the forgotten and the down-and-out, because that is exactly where the compassion of God flows.
blocks.es_reference: Jesús extendió esa misma preocupación al extranjero, al enfermo, y al preso. "Fui extranjero, y no me recogisteis... enfermo, y en la cárcel, y no me visitasteis," advirtió — enseñando que la compasión mostrada o negada a "uno de estos más pequeños" es mostrada o negada a Él. La bondad, entonces, no ha de reservarse para nuestros amigos e iguales, las personas que pueden recompensarnos. Ha de fluir especialmente hacia el olvidado y el caído, porque ahí es exactamente donde fluye la compasión de Dios.

blocks.en: 6. Kindness Is a Garment We Put On
blocks.es_reference: 6. La Bondad Es una Prenda Que Nos Ponemos

blocks.en: Colossians 3:12 (NKJV): "Therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, put on tender mercies, kindness, humility, meekness, longsuffering."
blocks.es_reference: Colosenses 3:12 (RVG): "Vestíos, pues, como escogidos de Dios, santos y amados, de entrañas de misericordia, de benignidad, de humildad, de mansedumbre, de paciencia."

blocks.en: Paul tells us to "put on" kindness, as one puts on a garment. The image is deliberate: kindness is something we choose to wear, intentionally, each day. This means we do not have to wait until we feel kind to act kindly. On the days when we are tired, irritable, or preoccupied, we can still deliberately clothe ourselves with kindness toward the people we meet — and very often the feeling follows the choice.
blocks.es_reference: Pablo nos dice que nos "vistamos" de benignidad, como uno se pone una prenda. La imagen es deliberada: la bondad es algo que elegimos vestir, intencionalmente, cada día. Esto significa que no tenemos que esperar a sentirnos bondadosos para actuar con bondad. En los días en que estamos cansados, irritables, o preocupados, todavía podemos deliberadamente revestirnos de bondad hacia las personas que encontramos — y muy a menudo el sentimiento sigue a la decisión.

blocks.en: This protects us from a common excuse. We tell ourselves that we are simply "not a naturally kind person," as though kindness were a fixed personality trait we either possess or lack. But Paul addresses kindness as a decision, a garment available to every believer to put on. The grumpiest among us can still choose, in a given moment, to speak gently, to be patient, to do the helpful thing. Character is built precisely by choosing kindness before we feel it, until the wearing of it becomes second nature.
blocks.es_reference: Esto nos protege de una excusa común. Nos decimos que sencillamente "no somos una persona naturalmente bondadosa," como si la bondad fuera un rasgo de personalidad fijo que poseemos o nos falta. Pero Pablo trata la bondad como una decisión, una prenda al alcance de todo creyente para ponérsela. El más gruñón de nosotros todavía puede elegir, en un momento dado, hablar con suavidad, ser paciente, hacer la cosa útil. El carácter se forma precisamente al elegir la bondad antes de sentirla, hasta que el vestirla se vuelve segunda naturaleza.

blocks.en: 7. Kindness Is Fruit, Not Willpower
blocks.es_reference: 7. La Bondad Es Fruto, No Fuerza de Voluntad

blocks.en: Galatians 5:22-23 (NKJV): "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control."
blocks.es_reference: Gálatas 5:22-23 (RVG): "Mas el fruto del Espíritu es amor, gozo, paz, paciencia, benignidad, bondad, fe, mansedumbre, templanza."

blocks.en: There is a deeper truth here that keeps the "put on kindness" command from becoming mere self-improvement. Paul lists kindness among the fruit of the Spirit — not the achievements of the flesh, but the fruit the Holy Spirit grows in a surrendered life. This means that genuine, lasting kindness is finally not something we manufacture by willpower at all; it is something God produces in us as we walk with Him.
blocks.es_reference: Hay una verdad más honda aquí que impide que el mandamiento de "vestirse de bondad" se vuelva mera superación personal. Pablo enumera la bondad entre el fruto del Espíritu — no los logros de la carne, sino el fruto que el Espíritu Santo cultiva en una vida rendida. Esto significa que la bondad genuina y duradera no es al final algo que fabricamos por fuerza de voluntad en absoluto; es algo que Dios produce en nosotros al caminar con Él.

blocks.en: Holding the two truths together keeps us balanced. On the one hand, we deliberately put on kindness, choosing it before we feel it. On the other hand, we depend on the Spirit to grow real kindness in us from the inside, knowing our own efforts will run dry. A branch does not strain to produce fruit; it simply stays connected to the vine, and the fruit comes. So with kindness: we keep choosing it, and we keep abiding in Christ, and the Spirit makes our chosen kindness into something genuine and deep, the very kindness of God flowing through us.
blocks.es_reference: Sostener juntas las dos verdades nos mantiene equilibrados. Por un lado, deliberadamente nos vestimos de bondad, eligiéndola antes de sentirla. Por otro lado, dependemos del Espíritu para cultivar bondad real en nosotros desde adentro, sabiendo que nuestros propios esfuerzos se secarán. Una rama no se esfuerza por producir fruto; sencillamente permanece conectada a la vid, y el fruto viene. Así con la bondad: seguimos eligiéndola, y seguimos permaneciendo en Cristo, y el Espíritu hace de nuestra bondad elegida algo genuino y hondo, la bondad misma de Dios fluyendo a través de nosotros.

blocks.en: 8. Kindness as Witness
blocks.es_reference: 8. La Bondad como Testimonio

blocks.en: A heart full of Christ's compassion becomes one of the most powerful testimonies in the world, especially in places of darkness. Kindness shines brightest against the blackest backgrounds, and the watching world cannot easily explain it away.
blocks.es_reference: Un corazón lleno de la compasión de Cristo se vuelve uno de los testimonios más poderosos del mundo, especialmente en lugares de oscuridad. La bondad brilla más intensamente contra los fondos más negros, y el mundo que observa no puede fácilmente explicarla.

blocks.en: Light in a Soviet prison: A man named Kozlov, once a criminal and later a church leader, wrote of life in a Soviet labor camp where prisoners often served sentences of twenty or twenty-five years. Amid the general despair — men cursing their fate, harming themselves, even taking their own lives — the Christians did not despair. Their pure and upright lives, their deep faith, and above all their gentleness toward others became, in his words, a shining example of real life for thousands. One could see Christ reflected in their faces. Their kindness in a place of cruelty preached more loudly than any sermon.
blocks.es_reference: Luz en una prisión soviética: Un hombre llamado Kozlov, una vez criminal y luego líder de iglesia, escribió de la vida en un campo de trabajo soviético donde los presos a menudo cumplían sentencias de veinte o veinticinco años. En medio de la desesperación general — hombres maldiciendo su suerte, haciéndose daño, hasta quitándose la vida — los cristianos no desesperaban. Sus vidas puras y rectas, su fe profunda, y sobre todo su gentileza hacia los demás se volvieron, en sus palabras, un ejemplo brillante de vida real para miles. Se podía ver a Cristo reflejado en sus rostros. Su bondad en un lugar de crueldad predicó más fuerte que cualquier sermón.

blocks.en: This is the radical reach of kindness: Jesus tells us that God Himself "is kind to the unthankful and evil," and calls us to be kind even to those who do not deserve it or return it. "Blessed are the merciful," He said, "for they shall obtain mercy." A kindness that extends only to the deserving is just ordinary fairness; the kindness of the kingdom reaches the ungrateful, the difficult, and the enemy — and in doing so it makes the invisible God strangely visible.
blocks.es_reference: Éste es el alcance radical de la bondad: Jesús nos dice que Dios mismo "es benigno para con los ingratos y malos," y nos llama a ser bondadosos aun con quienes no lo merecen ni lo devuelven. "Bienaventurados los misericordiosos," dijo, "porque ellos alcanzarán misericordia." Una bondad que se extiende solo a los que la merecen es apenas justicia ordinaria; la bondad del reino alcanza al ingrato, al difícil, y al enemigo — y al hacerlo hace al Dios invisible extrañamente visible.

blocks.en: 9. Be Moved, and Move
blocks.es_reference: 9. Sé Movido, y Muévete

blocks.en: So we come back to where we began, to Jesus looking out over the weary crowds and being moved with compassion. That is the pattern for every kind heart: first to be genuinely moved — to let the suffering of others register in us, to feel it, to say with Christ "I feel you" — and then to move, to let that feeling become a deed. Compassion that is only felt and never acted on dies in the heart; compassion that acts without feeling becomes cold duty. Real kindness holds both together: a heart that is moved, and hands that move.
blocks.es_reference: Así que volvemos a donde comenzamos, a Jesús contemplando las multitudes cansadas y siendo movido a compasión. Ése es el patrón para todo corazón bondadoso: primero ser genuinamente movido — dejar que el sufrimiento de los demás registre en nosotros, sentirlo, decir con Cristo "te siento" — y luego moverse, dejar que ese sentimiento se vuelva obra. La compasión que solo se siente y nunca se actúa muere en el corazón; la compasión que actúa sin sentir se vuelve deber frío. La bondad verdadera sostiene ambas cosas juntas: un corazón que es movido, y manos que se mueven.

blocks.en: To be kind, then, is nothing less than to share the heart of Christ. We put on kindness deliberately as a garment, we depend on the Spirit to grow it as fruit, we aim it especially at the overlooked and the undeserving, and we let it become our witness to a watching world. The God who was kind to us when we were unthankful and evil is at work to make us kind like Himself — people who, seeing the multitudes, are moved with compassion, and then get up and help.
blocks.es_reference: Ser bondadoso, entonces, no es nada menos que compartir el corazón de Cristo. Nos vestimos de bondad deliberadamente como una prenda, dependemos del Espíritu para cultivarla como fruto, la dirigimos especialmente al olvidado y al inmerecedor, y dejamos que se vuelva nuestro testimonio ante un mundo que observa. El Dios que fue bondadoso con nosotros cuando éramos ingratos y malos está obrando para hacernos bondadosos como Él mismo — personas que, viendo las multitudes, son movidas a compasión, y luego se levantan y ayudan.

mc.stem: In Matthew 9:36, how did Jesus see the multitudes?
options: As a problem to be managed
As weary and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd — and was moved with compassion
mc.why: Jesus saw the crowds not as a faceless mass but as weary, scattered people like sheep without a shepherd, and something moved in Him — compassion.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, how is biblical kindness different from mere politeness?
options: It is compassion — a heart that truly sees people's need and is stirred to help
mc.why: We often reduce kindness to politeness, but biblical kindness is weightier: compassion, a heart that truly sees people in their need and is stirred to help them.

mc.stem: What does the Gospel word for Jesus' 'compassion' actually mean?
options: To be moved viscerally, from the very core of one's being
mc.why: The word does not mean mild sympathy but to be moved viscerally, from the core of one's being; Jesus felt the people's pain in His gut.

mc.stem: How does the Spanish phrase 'lo siento' illustrate compassion in the lesson?
options: It literally means something like 'I feel it' — 'I feel it with you'
It has no connection to compassion
mc.why: 'Lo siento,' we translate 'I am sorry,' literally means closer to 'I feel it'; to say it to someone in pain is to say 'I feel it with you' — like Jesus, who felt their pain.

mc.stem: According to Ephesians 4:32, where does Christian kindness come from?
options: It overflows from the kindness God showed us — 'as God in Christ forgave you'
mc.why: Paul says be kind 'even as God in Christ forgave you'; our kindness is a reflection and overflow of the kindness God has already shown us.

mc.stem: The lesson says kindness is best understood as what?
options: A debt to earn God's favor
Gratitude in action — giving what we have received
mc.why: Kindness is not a debt to earn favor or a strain we manufacture; it is gratitude in action, the natural response of a heart treated far more kindly than it deserved.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, what does true compassion always become?
options: A deed — it never stays a feeling but always acts
mc.why: True compassion never stays a feeling; it always becomes a deed. When Jesus was moved, He healed, fed, and forgave; sentiment that does nothing is not real kindness.

mc.stem: How does the example of Caleb illustrate compassion that acts?
options: He gave a speech about kindness
He carried a plate of food to a man who couldn't walk, then bought him a Coke
mc.why: Caleb carried a plate of food to a man around the corner who couldn't walk, then bought him a Coke too — noticing a nearby need and meeting it, with thoughtfulness added.

mc.stem: What is the 'genius' of Christian kindness, according to the lesson?
options: It is available to everyone, all the time — take the small occasion and fill it with love
It is only for the wealthy
mc.why: We may not feed five thousand, but we can carry a plate to a neighbor; compassion that acts takes the small occasion at hand and fills it with love.

mc.stem: How does James 1:27 define 'pure and undefiled religion'?
options: By visiting orphans and widows in their trouble, and keeping unspotted from the world
mc.why: James defines pure religion not by ceremony or opinion but by looking after orphans and widows in distress — caring for those who can do nothing for us in return.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, what is the truest test of our kindness?
options: How kind we are to important people
How we treat those who can do nothing for us in return
mc.why: The truest test of kindness is how we treat those who can do nothing for us in return — the powerless, the forgotten, the down-and-out, where God's compassion flows.

mc.stem: In Matthew 25, what did Jesus teach about kindness to 'the least of these'?
options: Compassion shown or withheld to the least is shown or withheld to Him
mc.why: Jesus warned 'I was a stranger... sick and in prison and you did not visit Me,' teaching that compassion shown or withheld to the least of these is shown or withheld to Him.

mc.stem: What does Colossians 3:12 ('put on kindness') teach about being kind?
options: Kindness is a garment we deliberately put on, even before we feel it
Kindness is a fixed personality trait
mc.why: Paul says 'put on' kindness like a garment; we don't wait until we feel kind but deliberately clothe ourselves with it, and the feeling often follows the choice.

mc.stem: What common excuse does the 'put on kindness' command address?
options: That we are simply 'not a naturally kind person'
That only pastors must be kind
mc.why: We excuse ourselves as 'not naturally kind,' but Paul treats kindness as a decision available to every believer; even the grumpiest can choose to speak gently and help.

mc.stem: According to Galatians 5:22, what keeps 'put on kindness' from being mere self-improvement?
options: Kindness is fruit of the Spirit — God grows it in a surrendered life
mc.why: Kindness is listed among the fruit of the Spirit, not achievements of the flesh; lasting kindness is finally produced by God in us, not manufactured by willpower.

mc.stem: How does the lesson hold together 'put on kindness' and 'kindness is fruit'?
options: We deliberately choose kindness AND depend on the Spirit to grow it, like a branch abiding in the vine
mc.why: We keep choosing kindness before we feel it, and keep abiding in Christ; a branch doesn't strain to produce fruit but stays connected to the vine, and fruit comes.

mc.stem: How did the Christians in the Soviet prison (Kozlov's account) bear witness?
options: Amid despair, their gentleness and faith became a shining example of real life for thousands
mc.why: Amid despair where men cursed and harmed themselves, the Christians did not despair; their gentleness became a shining example of real life — one could see Christ in their faces.

mc.stem: According to Luke 6:35, to whom is God kind, and whom should we be kind to?
options: God is kind to the unthankful and evil; we are to be kind even to those who don't deserve it
mc.why: God is kind to the unthankful and evil, and calls us to be kind even to the ungrateful, difficult, and enemy; kindness only to the deserving is mere ordinary fairness.

mc.stem: What is the two-part pattern for a kind heart the lesson gives?
options: Be moved (feel it), and then move (let feeling become a deed)
mc.why: First be genuinely moved — feel the suffering, say 'I feel you' — then move, letting feeling become a deed; compassion only felt dies, compassion without feeling becomes cold duty.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, what is it ultimately to be kind?
options: Nothing less than to share the heart of Christ
mc.why: To be kind is nothing less than to share the heart of Christ: moved with compassion at the multitudes, and then getting up to help; God makes us kind like Himself.

fill.prompt: Jesus saw the multitudes as weary and scattered, "like sheep having no ____" (Matthew 9:36).
The word the Gospels use for Jesus' compassion means to be moved ____, from the very core of one's being.
Ephesians 4:32 says: "And be kind to one another, ____, forgiving one another, even as God in Christ forgave you."
Scripture says it is the kindness of God that leads us to ____.
Kindness is not a debt we pay to earn God's favor; it is ____ in action.
Feeling sorry for people while doing nothing is not biblical kindness; it is ____, which costs nothing and helps no one.
James 1:27 defines pure religion as visiting ____ and widows in their trouble.
Paul tells us to "put on" kindness, as one puts on the ____ we choose to wear each day.
Because kindness is fruit of the Spirit, lasting kindness is not something we manufacture by ____ but something God produces in us.

sa.prompt: Explain Matthew 9:36 and how Jesus' compassion reveals what kindness truly is.
sa.model: Before Jesus ever commands us to be kind, the Gospels show His own kindness in action, for again and again we read that He had compassion on them. He saw the multitudes not as a faceless crowd or a problem to be managed but as weary, scattered people, like sheep having no shepherd, and something moved in Him. Kindness in its deepest Christian sense begins not with a duty we perform but with a heart genuinely moved by the condition of others. This matters because we often reduce kindness to mere politeness or good manners, but the kindness Jesus models and commands is far weightier: it is compassion, a heart that truly sees people in their need and is stirred to help them. The crowds were harassed and helpless, and Jesus did not look past them or grow annoyed; He was moved for them, and to be kind is to let our hearts be moved as His was and then to act.

sa.prompt: Explain the meaning of biblical compassion using the 'lo siento / I feel you' insight.
sa.model: The word the Gospels use for Jesus' compassion is remarkably physical; it does not describe a mild sympathy or passing pity but means to be moved viscerally, from the very core of one's being, so that Jesus felt the people's pain in His gut. There is a beautiful picture of this in the Spanish phrase lo siento, which we translate I am sorry but which literally means something closer to I feel it. To say lo siento to someone in pain is to say I feel it with you, and in places of deep suffering people say much the same thing, I feel you. That is exactly what Jesus was like, for He felt their pain, and so His compassion was never abstract: when people were sick He healed them, when they were hungry He fed them, on one occasion more than five thousand, and when they were trapped in sin He forgave them. Compassion that truly feels will always move toward the one who hurts.

sa.prompt: Using Ephesians 4:32, explain where Christian kindness comes from and why that matters.
sa.model: We cannot understand the command to be kind until we see where Christian kindness comes from. Paul does not simply say be kind; he says be kind to one another even as God in Christ forgave you, so our kindness is meant to be a reflection and overflow of the kindness God has already shown us. Scripture says it is the kindness of God that leads us to repentance, that we love because He first loved us and are kind because He was first kind to us. This changes how we approach the command, for kindness is not a debt we pay to earn God's favor nor a strain we manufacture by gritted teeth. It is gratitude in action, the natural response of a heart treated far more kindly than it deserved. When we remember how patient and merciful God has been with us in Christ, kindness toward others stops feeling like a burden and becomes the most reasonable thing in the world, for we give what we have received.

sa.prompt: Explain why true compassion must act, using the example of Caleb.
sa.model: True compassion never stays a feeling; it always becomes a deed, for when Jesus was moved with compassion He did something about it, healing, feeding, and forgiving. Feeling sorry for people while doing nothing is not the kindness Scripture commends but sentiment, and sentiment costs nothing and helps no one, while the kindness God calls for gets up off its chair. Kindness like this is usually unspectacular and close to home. A young man named Caleb knew of a man around the corner who could not walk, so he carried a plate of food down to him and then went back out and bought him a Coke as well, with no grand program and no fanfare, just a person who noticed a nearby need and met it with a little extra thoughtfulness. We may not be able to feed five thousand, but we can carry a plate to a neighbor; compassion that acts does not wait for a great occasion but takes the small occasion at hand and fills it with love.

sa.prompt: How does James 1:27 and Matthew 25 show kindness toward the overlooked?
sa.model: Scripture has a special concern for the people the world tends to overlook. From the days of Moses the widow and the orphan were placed under God's particular protection and commended to the tender care of the righteous, and James defines pure religion not by ceremony or correct opinion but by looking after orphans and widows in their distress. The truest test of our kindness is how we treat those who can do nothing for us in return, the people with no power, no status, and nothing to offer. Jesus extended the same concern to the stranger, the sick, and the prisoner, warning I was a stranger and you did not take Me in, I was sick and in prison and you did not visit Me, teaching that compassion shown or withheld to the least of these is shown or withheld to Him. Kindness is therefore not reserved for friends and equals who can repay us but flows especially toward the forgotten and the down-and-out, because that is where the compassion of God flows.

sa.prompt: Explain Colossians 3:12 and how kindness can be a garment we choose to wear.
sa.model: Paul tells us to put on kindness as one puts on a garment, and the image is deliberate, for kindness is something we choose to wear intentionally each day. This means we do not have to wait until we feel kind to act kindly; on the days when we are tired, irritable, or preoccupied, we can still deliberately clothe ourselves with kindness toward the people we meet, and very often the feeling follows the choice. This protects us from a common excuse, for we tell ourselves we are simply not a naturally kind person, as though kindness were a fixed personality trait we either possess or lack. But Paul addresses kindness as a decision, a garment available to every believer to put on, so even the grumpiest among us can choose in a given moment to speak gently, to be patient, and to do the helpful thing. Character is built precisely by choosing kindness before we feel it, until the wearing of it becomes second nature.

sa.prompt: Explain Galatians 5:22 and how kindness as 'fruit' balances kindness as a choice.
sa.model: There is a deeper truth that keeps the put on kindness command from becoming mere self-improvement, for Paul lists kindness among the fruit of the Spirit, not the achievements of the flesh but the fruit the Holy Spirit grows in a surrendered life. This means genuine, lasting kindness is finally not something we manufacture by willpower at all but something God produces in us as we walk with Him. Holding the two truths together keeps us balanced: on the one hand we deliberately put on kindness, choosing it before we feel it, and on the other hand we depend on the Spirit to grow real kindness in us from the inside, knowing our own efforts will run dry. A branch does not strain to produce fruit but simply stays connected to the vine, and the fruit comes; so with kindness, we keep choosing it and keep abiding in Christ, and the Spirit makes our chosen kindness into something genuine and deep, the very kindness of God flowing through us.

sa.prompt: Using the Kozlov account, explain how kindness becomes a witness.
sa.model: A heart full of Christ's compassion becomes one of the most powerful testimonies in the world, especially in places of darkness, for kindness shines brightest against the blackest backgrounds and the watching world cannot easily explain it away. A man named Kozlov, once a criminal and later a church leader, wrote of life in a Soviet labor camp where prisoners often served sentences of twenty or twenty-five years. Amid the general despair, where men cursed their fate, harmed themselves, and even took their own lives, the Christians did not despair, and their pure and upright lives, deep faith, and above all their gentleness toward others became a shining example of real life for thousands, so that one could see Christ reflected in their faces. Their kindness in a place of cruelty preached more loudly than any sermon, showing the radical reach of a compassion that makes the invisible God strangely visible.

sa.prompt: According to Luke 6:35, how far does kingdom kindness reach, and why?
sa.model: Kindness in the kingdom of God reaches further than ordinary human kindness, for Jesus tells us that God Himself is kind to the unthankful and evil and calls us to be kind even to those who do not deserve it or return it. A kindness that extends only to the deserving is just ordinary fairness, the kind even pagans practice, but the kindness of the kingdom reaches the ungrateful, the difficult, and the enemy. Blessed are the merciful, Jesus said, for they shall obtain mercy, and in showing mercy to those who cannot repay it we reflect the very heart of God who showed mercy to us when we were His enemies. This is why such kindness makes the invisible God strangely visible: it cannot be explained by self-interest or by the ordinary calculations of the world, and so it points beyond itself to the God whose kindness has no limit and no condition.

sa.prompt: Summarize the two-part pattern of a kind heart and what it ultimately means to be kind.
sa.model: We come back to where we began, to Jesus looking out over the weary crowds and being moved with compassion, for that is the pattern for every kind heart: first to be genuinely moved, to let the suffering of others register in us, to feel it, to say with Christ I feel you, and then to move, to let that feeling become a deed. Compassion that is only felt and never acted on dies in the heart, while compassion that acts without feeling becomes cold duty, so real kindness holds both together, a heart that is moved and hands that move. To be kind, then, is nothing less than to share the heart of Christ. We put on kindness deliberately as a garment, we depend on the Spirit to grow it as fruit, we aim it especially at the overlooked and the undeserving, and we let it become our witness to a watching world, as the God who was kind to us when we were unthankful makes us kind like Himself.
